section.title: The Lord Reigns in Majesty
section.sectionRationale: The first of a cluster of enthronement psalms in Book IV, this brief but majestic song declares that the LORD reigns, robed in strength, His throne established from eternity, and mightier than the roaring floods, a kingship exercised directly by Christ when He commands the storm to be still.
section.thesis: The LORD reigns, robed in majesty and strength, His throne fixed from everlasting, and though the floodwaters roar, He is mightier still, a truth confirmed when Jesus Christ Himself commands the wind and the waves with the same divine authority this psalm ascribes to God alone.
section.frameNote: Three brief movements: the LORD's eternal, unshakeable reign, verses 1-2; the roaring floods lifting their voice, verse 3; and God's greater majesty above the waters, together with His sure and holy decrees, verses 4-5.

verses.text: The LORD {{malak|reigns}}! He is robed in majesty; the LORD has clothed and armed Himself with {{oz|strength}}. The world indeed is firmly established; it cannot be moved.
Your throne was established long ago; You are from all eternity.

units.label: The Floods Have Lifted Their Voice

verses.text: The floodwaters have risen, O LORD; the rivers have raised their voice; the seas lift up their pounding waves.

units.label: The Lord on High Is Majestic
units.note: God's sure decrees and holy house

verses.text: Above the roar of {{mayim|many waters}}, the mighty breakers of the sea, the LORD on high is majestic.
Your {{edut|testimonies}} are fully confirmed; holiness adorns Your house, O LORD, for all the days to come.

malak.gloss: To reign, to be king. The psalm opens with this verb in a form emphasizing an already settled, present reality: the LORD is reigning now, not merely someday.

oz.gloss: Strength, might. God is pictured clothing Himself in this strength as a king dons royal robes, the very power that makes the created world firm and unshakeable.

mayim.gloss: Many waters, a common ancient Near Eastern picture of chaos and overwhelming threat. The psalm declares the LORD's majesty greater than even the mightiest, most chaotic breakers of the sea.

edut.gloss: Testimonies, solemn decrees or laws. These trustworthy decrees of God are as firm and unshakeable as His throne and the world He has established.

basic.context: This brief, majestic psalm declares that the LORD reigns, robed in strength, His throne fixed since before time began. Though the floodwaters roar and the seas lift their pounding waves, a picture of overwhelming chaos, the LORD on high remains mightier still.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm describes a present, settled reality, that God reigns now, not only in some future age, and it prescribes an abiding response: confident trust in God's unshaken sovereignty regardless of how chaotic or threatening present circumstances appear.
basic.originalLanguages: The psalm opens declaring the LORD malak, reigns, verse 1, clothed in oz, strength. Even the roaring of mayim rabbim, many waters, a common picture of chaos, verse 4, cannot overcome His majesty, and His edut, testimonies or decrees, verse 5, are as firm as His throne.
basic.typology: The LORD's mastery over the roaring floods and pounding waves anticipates Christ's own authority over the storm, when He rebukes wind and sea with the same divine command this psalm ascribes to God alone.
basic.christ: When Jesus stood in the boat and said to the wind and waves, 'Peace, be still,' and the storm obeyed Him completely, He exercised the very authority this psalm attributes to the LORD, showing Himself to be the reigning God enthroned above every chaotic power, Mark 4:39.
basic.god: God is shown reigning already, robed in majesty and strength, His throne established before the world itself, greater than every roaring flood or pounding wave, and utterly reliable in both His decrees and the holiness of His dwelling.
basic.crossReferences: Mark 4:35-41 records Jesus commanding the storm to be still with the very authority this psalm ascribes to God. Colossians 1:17 says in Christ all things hold together. Revelation 19:6 pictures praise like the roar of many waters before God's throne.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's declaration that the LORD reigns above every roaring chaos finds its living demonstration in Christ, who commands the wind and waves as God alone can, and in whom all things, however threatening they seem, are held firmly together.

context.literary:
Psalm 93 has only five verses, and it is shaped so that the smallest details carry the weight. It has a clear centre. Verses 1 and 2 describe the throne, verse 3 describes the threat, and verses 4 and 5 describe the answer. The threat gets a full verse to itself. The psalm does not pretend that the danger is small. It gives the floods their turn, and it gives them a turn of their own rhythm, for the word for the waters is repeated three times in a row in verse 3, each time with the verb "lifted up." The line builds like a wave. Then verse 4 sets a single line of the LORD against it.

The opening is dressed like a coronation. The LORD is "robed in majesty," He is "clothed" and "armed" with strength, and the picture is of a king in his robes and belt. The psalm then turns at once to the world: "The world indeed is firmly established; it cannot be moved." The same idea of firmness is stated of the throne in verse 2, "established long ago," and of the decrees in verse 5, "fully confirmed." The three firm things, the world, the throne and the word, hold each other up.

The voice of the psalm changes in a quiet way. Verse 1 speaks about the LORD in the third person, as a herald would announce a king. Verse 2 turns to address Him directly, "Your throne," and the address continues in verse 3, "O LORD," and in verse 5, "Your testimonies." The announcement has become a prayer. The psalm also holds a second contrast, between the roar and the majesty. Verse 4 says God is "majestic," and uses the same Hebrew word that it uses for the "mighty" breakers, so that He is called mighty in the very word that describes the waves, and it is His might that is greater.

Psalm 93 is also the first of a group. The cry "The LORD reigns" opens Psalms 93, 97 and 99 and runs through 95 to 99, so that this short psalm is the gate to a whole section of the Psalter that celebrates the kingship of God.
context.historical:
The Hebrew text gives Psalm 93 no title, but the ancient Greek translation does: it calls it a song "for the day before the Sabbath, when the earth was founded." The link is with creation, the sixth day, and Jewish tradition remembers the psalm as the one sung on Friday in the temple service, the day before the Sabbath psalm that stands just ahead of it in our Bibles. The two psalms belong together as the close of the week and the day of rest.

The watery imagery had a setting in Israel's neighbours' stories. In the texts from ancient Ugarit, the storm god Baal fights Prince Sea and Judge River, and those powers are hostile to the gods. The poet here uses the same words, rivers and seas, and puts them in a very different story. There is no battle in the psalm. The waters roar, but the LORD does not have to wrestle with them. He is simply "majestic" above them. Israel's poets keep the old picture of the sea as chaos and take the drama away, because in Israel's faith the sea is something God made, Genesis 1:9-10, and something He governs, Job 38:8-11.

The floods had also been real events. Israel remembered the Flood, when the fountains of the great deep burst forth, Genesis 7:11, and the crossing of the sea with walls of water on either side, Exodus 14:21-22. The prophets used the sea as an image of nations: "the tumult of many peoples; they rage like the roaring seas," Isaiah 17:12-13. A nation under threat from Assyria, Babylon or Egypt would hear the roar in verse 3 as a description of politics as well as weather.

The last verse looks at the sanctuary. The "testimonies" are the covenant words kept in the ark of the Testimony, where God said He would meet with His people, Exodus 25:22. Holiness "adorns" the house, which was the place where God's rule was focused on earth for Israel.
context.canonical:
Psalm 93 is the keystone of Book IV's answer to Book III. Psalm 89 ends with the Davidic king cast down and the throne seemingly lost. Psalms 90 to 92 carry the people through judgment, shelter and Sabbath joy, and Psalm 93 states the conclusion they were heading for: "The LORD reigns!" The rule of God does not depend on the throne of David, and it does not depend on Israel's circumstances. The group that follows, Psalms 95 to 99, builds the same shout into a whole liturgy, and Psalm 96:10 repeats almost word for word the claim of verse 1, "The world is firmly established; it cannot be moved."

The psalm also reaches back to Moses. Moses' song after the crossing of the sea ended with "The LORD will reign forever and ever," Exodus 15:18, and Psalm 93 takes up that line for a people who have to live between crossings. The eternity of verse 2 echoes Psalm 90:2, where God was God "from everlasting to everlasting." The floods echo Psalm 29, where the LORD "sits enthroned over the flood," Psalm 29:10, and Psalm 89:9, "You rule the raging sea." In Psalm 65:7 He "stilled the roaring of the seas, the pounding of their waves, and the tumult of the nations."

The New Testament shows the same God at work in Jesus. When Jesus commands the sea in Mark 4:39, the disciples ask, "Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?" Mark 4:41, and the Old Testament already has the answer. Hebrews says the Son upholds all things by His powerful word, Hebrews 1:3, and Paul says "in Him all things hold together," Colossians 1:17, which is the claim of verse 1 that the world cannot be moved. Revelation picks up the psalm's language at its climax: "the Lord our God the Almighty reigns," and the sound of the worshipers is "like the rushing of many waters," Revelation 19:6.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist wanted God's people to begin from the right fact. Whatever they saw around them, the kingdom was already settled. "The LORD reigns" is not a hope about the end of history but a report of how things are, and everything else in the psalm is to be read from there. This matters because Israel's experience gave them constant reasons to think otherwise: armies, exile, the fall of kings, storms and losses. The psalm does not deny the roar. It gives the roar its full verse and then says something greater is above it.

The author also wanted to shape worship. A short psalm can be learned by heart and said in the night, and a people who could say "the LORD reigns" together were taught to stand on it in trouble. The last verse turns that confidence toward the house of the LORD. The God who reigns has made His word reliable and His house holy, and those are the two things that a people in a shaking world can keep close.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes the reality of God's reign, and it prescribes confidence in it, but it does not promise that believers will never be in the water. The disciples were in a boat that was being swamped, Mark 4:37, and Jesus was in the boat with them. Paul's ship was battered for many days until "we abandoned all hope of being saved," Acts 27:20, and yet God brought him through. The psalm never says the floods do not rise. It says that they are not the highest thing.

The imagery also calls for some care in use. Not every difficulty is a hostile power, and not every political crisis is the roar of the sea raging against God. To apply the psalm is to say to oneself in fear, as the psalmist does, that the LORD is on high and that He reigns, and to hold that truth when the evidence of the moment seems against it. It is not a licence to treat every opponent as chaos to be dismissed. The psalm teaches dependence, not triumphalism. It is a psalm to be said with the feet on wet ground.

debates.question: Does the roaring of the floodwaters in verse 3 refer to literal natural chaos, hostile nations, or both?

views.label: It refers primarily to literal, natural chaos, echoing ancient pictures of the sea as untamed power
views.case: The vocabulary of floods, rivers, and pounding waves closely parallels other psalms describing literal cosmic and natural forces, such as Psalm 29 and Psalm 46, which the LORD is shown to master by His voice alone.

views.label: It functions symbolically for raging, hostile nations and political turmoil
views.case: Elsewhere in the Psalms, 'many waters' and roaring seas serve as stock imagery for hostile, chaotic nations rising against God's people, so this psalm may be reassuring Israel amid genuine political threat as much as natural upheaval.

debates.bearing: Either way, the psalm's confidence holds: whatever roars, whether nature or nations, cannot overcome the LORD's settled and eternal reign, a truth Christ Himself later enacted literally over both a storm and every hostile power.

debates.question: Is 'The LORD reigns' in verse 1 an announcement of a new enthronement or a statement of a standing fact?

views.label: He has become king
views.case: The Hebrew verb is the kind that can mean 'has taken the throne,' and the cry sounds like a coronation shout. Some scholars hold that Israel celebrated God's kingship at a yearly festival where the people proclaimed it afresh, and that this psalm belongs to such an occasion.

views.label: He reigns, and always has
views.case: Verse 2 says the throne was established 'long ago' and that God is 'from all eternity,' and verse 1 says the world is firmly established. Nothing is being won in the psalm. On this view the cry is a proclamation of what is already true and must be told again to those who forget.

views.label: Both, in different senses
views.case: The kingship is eternal, but it is repeatedly made visible in history, at the sea, at Sinai and in the temple. Each time the people cry 'The LORD reigns' they recognise it afresh, and the New Testament speaks the same way, as when the seventh trumpet announces that the kingdom of the world 'has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ,' Revelation 11:15.

debates.bearing: The second view suits the text best, and the third explains why the cry could be used in worship and again in the Revelation. God is not made king by the psalm. The psalm says it so that His people may live as those whose king is already on the throne.

debates.question: Are the floods in verse 3 rebels or worshipers?

views.label: Rebels
views.case: The floods are the hostile force that the poem sets against the LORD, and they are 'mighty' and pounding. The wicked are called 'the storm-tossed sea' in Isaiah 57:20, and many peoples roar like seas in Isaiah 17:12-13. On this view the waters of verse 3 stand for everything in creation and politics that opposes God's rule.

views.label: Worshipers in a wrong voice
views.case: The waters 'raise their voice,' and in other psalms the sea and the rivers do lift their voice in praise: 'Let the sea resound... let the rivers clap their hands,' Psalm 98:7-8. Some readers hear in verse 3 a foretaste of that, where creation makes a noise and only the LORD on high makes the right sense of it.

views.label: Dangerous but created
views.case: The waters are neither rebels with a will of their own nor singers. They are the raw power of God's own creation, and they roar because that is their nature. The LORD is over them as the Creator is over His work, Psalm 104:6-9.

debates.bearing: The first view fits the immediate danger in the psalm, and the second and third remind us that the LORD has no rival. Whichever is preferred, the verse says that the power of the sea is real and that its voice is less than His.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 says the LORD is "robed in majesty." The word for majesty is ge'ut, from a root that means to rise up or be exalted. The next phrase says He "has clothed and armed Himself with strength." The second verb is a form of the verb for girding, to tie on a belt, which is what a man does before work or war. God is pictured both as a king in robes and as a worker with his belt fastened. Majesty and strength are not things He has but things He wears.

The verb "established" appears twice and is the same verb family that ends Psalm 90. In verse 1 "firmly established" is tikkon, and in verse 2 "established" is nakhon, both from kun, and Psalm 90:17 closes with Moses' prayer that God would "establish" the work of our hands, using the same root twice. The prayer for something to last is answered in a psalm about the firmest thing there is. Verse 1 adds that the world "cannot be moved," from a verb that means to totter or be shaken, used of the righteous who will never be shaken.

The great phrase of verse 2, "from all eternity You are," uses the word olam with the preposition "from," so that it reads "from everlasting You." It is nearly the language of Psalm 90:2, "from everlasting to everlasting You are God," as if the psalm were quoting it. The throne was set "long ago," a word that means from that time back, but God Himself is beyond every "long ago."

The verb "lifted up" in verse 3 is nasa, and it is repeated three times with the word for rivers, neharot. The same verb is used in Psalm 24 of lifting up the gates and in the priestly blessing of lifting up the countenance, so it is a word that can mean exaltation. The same verb that belongs to worship is used of the waves. The word "pounding" comes from a root for crushing, and it is an image of waves that break and grind.

Verse 4 uses the word addir for "mighty" and "majestic." It appears twice in the verse, once for the breakers and once for the LORD, and the repetition is the whole argument. The waters are addir, and He is addir on high, marom, the word for the heights. The contrast is one of height and not of kind.

In verse 5 "fully confirmed" is ne'emnu, from aman, the root that gives us "amen" and "faithfulness," so that the testimonies are declared amen, firm and trustworthy. "Adorns" is na'avah, a word of fitting beauty, used in Psalm 33:1 of praise that is fitting for the upright. Holiness is the right dress for God's house as majesty is for His person.

typology.type: The LORD who stills the sea, Psalm 93:3-4
typology.fulfillment: The Old Testament already says that only God can quiet the waves: 'You rule the raging sea; when its waves mount up, You still them,' Psalm 89:9, and 'He calmed the storm to a whisper,' Psalm 107:29. In the boat on Galilee, Jesus 'rebuked the wind and the sea,' and the disciples ask, 'Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?' Mark 4:39-41. The correspondence is between the God above the flood and the Man in the stern. The escalation is that He does it with a word and from inside the boat. The type falls short of the end, for storms still come and the final calming awaits the new creation.

typology.type: The One who treads on the sea, Psalm 93:4
typology.fulfillment: Job says that God 'alone stretches out the heavens and treads on the waves of the sea,' Job 9:8, and Psalm 77:19 says His path led through the sea. In Matthew, Jesus goes out to His disciples 'walking on the sea,' says 'Take courage! It is I,' and Peter and the others worship Him, saying 'Truly You are the Son of God!' Matthew 14:25-33. The correspondence is of a divine act and a human body. The escalation is that Peter is called to share it by faith. The pattern does not make Christians walk on water, but it shows that the waters lie under the feet of the one they trust.

typology.type: The throne established long ago, Psalm 93:2
typology.fulfillment: The eternal throne of the LORD meets the promised throne of David's son. Gabriel says, 'The Lord God will give Him the throne of His father David, and He will reign over the house of Jacob forever,' Luke 1:32-33, and Hebrews applies the psalm's language of an everlasting throne to the Son: 'Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever,' Hebrews 1:8. Jesus said, 'All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me,' Matthew 28:18. The type is a throne that never moves, and the escalation is that God's own reign is now exercised through a man who has been raised and seated at His right hand, Ephesians 1:20-22.

Holiness adorns the house of the LORD, the place where His testimonies rested, Exodus 25:22. Jesus says of His own body, 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again,' John 2:19-21, and Paul says the church is God's temple, 'and God's Spirit dwells in you,' 1 Corinthians 3:16-17. The house moves from stone to a Person and then to a people. The correspondence is of God's holy presence on earth. The escalation is that the presence is no longer in one place. The type is incomplete until the new Jerusalem, where no temple is needed because God is there.

The roar of many waters, which in the psalm is a threat, changes its character in the New Testament. The risen Christ has a voice 'like the roar of many waters,' Revelation 1:15, and the worship of the redeemed is 'like the rushing of many waters,' Revelation 19:6. The same sound that frightened Israel becomes the sound of the King and of those who praise Him. This is an echo and not a stated fulfilment, but it fits the direction of the psalm. The peoples who roar like seas, Revelation 17:15, are finally gathered into the worship of the one who sits above them, Revelation 7:9.

study.christ:
Psalm 93 leads to Christ by showing what the New Testament says He does. The clearest place is the Gospel of Mark, where Jesus is asleep in the stern while the wind and the waves break into the boat. The disciples wake Him and say, "Teacher, don't You care that we are perishing?" He gets up, "rebuked the wind and the sea," and says, "Silence! Be still!" Mark 4:38-39. The disciples do not ask what happened but who He is: "Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?" Mark 4:41. The psalms have already told them. Psalm 89:9 says of the LORD, "You rule the raging sea; when its waves mount up, You still them," and Psalm 107:29 says, "He calmed the storm to a whisper." Psalm 93 says the LORD on high is greater than the breakers. The disciples are in a boat with the One who fits that description.

The walking on the sea in Matthew 14 makes the same claim by a different act. Job 9:8 says God "treads on the waves of the sea," and Jesus comes to the disciples on the water with the words "Take courage! It is I," which some hear as an echo of the divine "I am". The boat then worships Him, "Truly You are the Son of God!" Matthew 14:27-33.

The psalm's confidence in an established throne is given a face in the exalted Christ. "The Son is the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature, upholding all things by His powerful word," Hebrews 1:3. "He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together," Colossians 1:17. These texts say of the Son what verse 1 says of the LORD, that the world does not move because the King upholds it. Jesus says, "All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me," Matthew 28:18, and Paul says God seated Him "far above all rule and authority," Ephesians 1:20-21. The kingdom of the psalm is His.

There is also a place for the floods in His own story. Psalm 69 speaks of waters up to the neck and deep waters where the flood engulfs, Psalm 69:1-2, and the Gospels show Jesus in Gethsemane and on the cross under a surge that He did not calm. The floods lifted their voice against Him, and in His resurrection the LORD on high proved majestic. The same Christ who stilled the storm went into the deep, and came out of it.

Finally, the psalm says God's testimonies are "fully confirmed." Paul writes that "all the promises of God are 'Yes' in Christ," and through Him our "Amen" is spoken, 2 Corinthians 1:20. The word that means confirmed in verse 5 is the root of "amen," and Christ is the Amen.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The psalm was not written as a forecast of the Galilean storm, and the New Testament does not treat it so. What the Gospels do is show the Son doing the things that the Old Testament reserves for the LORD, and the psalm supplies the language in which the disciples' question is answered.
study.god:
The first thing this psalm shows about God is that He is king now. The word is not "will reign" but "reigns," and it is said before anything else is said. The psalm wants its hearers to take that as the ground on which they stand, not as a belief to be defended. His reign is shown in His dress: He is "robed in majesty" and "armed with strength." The clothing is His own, and it is shown to be the kind that a king wears when he is in full command.

He is eternal. The throne was "established long ago," and He is "from all eternity." The psalm contrasts Him with everything that is made. The world is firmly established, but it is established by Him, and He is before it. This is the same eternity that Psalm 90 confessed before the mountains were born, and it is the reason the world cannot be moved. Its stability is borrowed from His.

He is greater than chaos without being its rival. The floods are not a second god. They roar, and the roar is real, and yet they are not the highest thing. "Above the roar of many waters, the mighty breakers of the sea, the LORD on high is majestic." The God of this psalm does not need to fight the sea to win. His majesty is already settled. That is a striking difference from the stories of Israel's neighbours, in which the gods contend with the waters. It reflects a God who made the sea and rules it without effort.

He is also near. The height in verse 4 is not distance, for verse 5 speaks of "Your house," where His testimonies are kept and holiness adorns the place. The God who rules the flood lives in a sanctuary among His people and speaks words that stand. The decrees are trustworthy because they come from the throne that cannot be moved, and this ties His sovereignty to His word. A king whose word could not be relied on would be no comfort in a flood.

He is holy. Holiness is what suits His house, and the word "adorns" says that holiness is not a burden for the house but its beauty. Worship in such a place is not fear of a storm. It is the fitting response to beauty and to power that is never misused.

The psalm also holds a tension without resolving it. God reigns, and yet the floods rise. Three times the waters lift their voice in a single verse, and the psalm does not pretend otherwise. The answer is not that the floods cease but that they are below Him. This is how the Bible speaks of trouble throughout: the threat is real and the King is greater.

For worship, the psalm shows where to stand. A person or a congregation in a shaking time can say these five verses aloud and be steadied by them. The right response is to praise a God who reigns, to trust His word, and to go to His house as those who know that the sea does not have the last word.

crossReferences.note: Moses confessed that God was God 'from everlasting to everlasting,' before the mountains were born. Psalm 93:2 takes the same eternity and sets it under a throne: 'You are from all eternity.' The wilderness prayer and the kingship psalm are joined by the same claim about who God is.

The LORD 'sits enthroned over the flood; the LORD is enthroned as King forever.' It is the clearest parallel to verses 3 and 4, where the floods roar and the LORD is enthroned above them. Both psalms say the flood does not unseat the king.

'You rule the raging sea; when its waves mount up, You still them.' The Davidic psalm that ends Book III makes the same statement about God's rule over the sea. Psalm 93, in Book IV, puts the claim in the present tense and shows that it still holds when the throne of David has fallen.

God 'stilled the roaring of the seas, the pounding of their waves, and the tumult of the nations.' The verse joins the sea and the nations in one line, which is how verse 3 can be read as speaking of both weather and world powers. It shows that the same God quiets both.

God asks Job who shut the sea behind doors and said, 'You may come this far, but no farther; here your proud waves must stop.' The floods of Psalm 93 have a limit set by their Maker, which is the ground of the psalm's confidence.

The prophet hears 'the tumult of many peoples' who 'rage like the roaring seas,' and says God rebukes them so that they flee like chaff. It shows how the roar of many waters became a picture of hostile nations, and how God's rebuke is the answer.

After the sea has swallowed Pharaoh's army, Moses sings, 'The LORD will reign forever and ever!' Psalm 93 is the later echo of that line for a people who keep meeting new waters. The God who reigned at the sea reigns still, and always will.

'Declare among the nations: The LORD reigns! The world is firmly established; it cannot be moved.' The verse is almost the same words as Psalm 93:1. The kingship proclamation that begins here is given to the nations in the psalms that follow.

Jesus rebukes the wind and the sea, and the disciples ask who He is. The psalm is the background to their question. Only the LORD, who is majestic above the breakers, does what Jesus has just done, and the Gospel is asking its readers to draw the conclusion.

Jesus walks on the sea and calls Peter to join Him. The waters that roar in Psalm 93 are under His feet and then under Peter's, until Peter sees the wind. The disciples worship Him as the Son of God, which is what the psalm would lead one to do.

John sees the risen Christ and hears His voice 'like the roar of many waters.' The sound that Israel feared is now the voice of the Son. It shows that the authority over the waters belongs to Him and that He speaks with it.

The worship of the redeemed sounds 'like the rushing of many waters,' and the cry is 'Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns.' It is Psalm 93:1 taken up by the whole multitude at the end. The roar has become praise.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 93 stands at the point where the Bible's story of water and kingship meets. The Bible begins with "darkness over the surface of the deep" and the Spirit of God "hovering over the surface of the waters," Genesis 1:2. The deep is there from the first verse, unformed and unruled, and the first acts of God are to speak into it, to gather the waters, and to call the dry land out. The seas are in the world from the start as something that God has set in order, and the psalm's claim that the LORD is greater than the breakers is the ordering of Genesis 1 still standing.

The fall let the waters back in as a threat. In the Flood, "all the fountains of the great deep burst forth," Genesis 7:11, and creation was undone. The exodus and the crossing of the Jordan show the waters held back for a redeemed people, Exodus 14:21-22 and Joshua 3:15-16. Israel's poets and prophets then turn the sea into a picture of the nations that threaten them, and the fourth beast of Daniel rises out of the great sea, Daniel 7:2-3. Psalm 93 is the confession that keeps Israel steady through all of it: the floods rise, and the LORD on high is greater.

The psalm sets up the kingship cry of Book IV, which reaches toward the nations, "Declare among the nations: The LORD reigns!" Psalm 96:10. It also sets up the New Testament. The Son steps into the boat and stills the water, walks over it and, in the end, goes down into the deeper flood of death and comes up again. Revelation shows the beast rising out of the sea, Revelation 13:1, as a last form of the old threat, but the same book says that the ancient serpent, who sends out water like a river, cannot sweep away the woman, for the earth swallows it, Revelation 12:15-16.

The new creation answers the psalm. John sees "a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and earth had passed away, and the sea was no more," Revelation 21:1. The restless sea is gone. In its place, before the throne, he sees "something like a sea of glass, as clear as crystal," Revelation 4:6, and the victorious stand beside it holding harps, Revelation 15:2. The water that once roared lies still under the throne. The throne that the psalm said was established long ago is now seen by all, the world is firmly established, and the roar that remains is the sound of many waters, which is the voice of the multitude crying that the Lord our God the Almighty reigns.

quiz.q: What does verse 1 declare about the LORD's reign?

options.text: That He reigns now, robed in majesty and strength, and the world is firmly established.
options.note: The psalm opens with a present, settled declaration of God's kingship, not a future hope only.

options.text: That His reign will only begin at some distant future date.
options.note: The psalm declares the LORD reigns now, in the present, not only in the future.

options.text: That His reign is uncertain and contested.
options.note: The psalm expresses total confidence, not uncertainty, about God's kingship.

options.text: That the world was created by God's power.
options.note: This is true and related, but verse 1's specific emphasis is that the world is firmly established and cannot be moved, not merely that God created it.

quiz.q: How long has God's throne been established, according to verse 2?

options.text: Long ago; God is from all eternity.
options.note: Verse 2 grounds God's kingship in His eternal existence, before time itself.

options.text: Only since the reign of King David.
options.note: The psalm speaks of eternity, far preceding any human king's reign.

options.text: It was established only recently.
options.note: The psalm explicitly says God's throne was established long ago, from all eternity.

options.text: It was established before the foundations of the world.
options.note: This is true and consistent with verse 2's eternity language, though it rephrases rather than using the psalm's own words, 'from all eternity.'

quiz.q: What image does verse 3 use to describe overwhelming chaos?

options.text: Rising floodwaters, roaring rivers, and pounding sea waves.
options.note: The verse's triple repetition builds the sense of relentless, mounting natural chaos.

options.text: A gentle, quiet stream.
options.note: The imagery is one of overwhelming, roaring chaos, not gentle calm.

options.text: A quiet desert with no water at all.
options.note: The imagery centers entirely on overwhelming waters, not dry desert.

options.text: Rising waters growing louder and more powerful.
options.note: This is very close to correct and captures the verse's escalating imagery, though the specific words are floodwaters, rivers, and pounding sea waves.

quiz.q: According to verse 4, who is greater than the roar of many waters?

options.text: The LORD on high, who is majestic above every mighty breaker of the sea.
options.note: This verse directly declares God's supremacy over even the most overwhelming natural chaos.

options.text: No one; the waters remain uncontrolled forever.
options.note: The verse explicitly declares the LORD's majesty as greater than the waters.

options.text: A pagan sea god from a neighboring nation.
options.note: The psalm names the LORD alone as supreme, directly countering ancient pagan myths of rival sea gods.

options.text: God's strength, robed in majesty since the beginning.
options.note: This is true and closely related to verse 1's language, though verse 4 specifically names the LORD's majesty as greater than the roar of many waters and the mighty breakers of the sea.

quiz.q: How does this psalm's picture of God's mastery over the waters connect to the New Testament?

options.text: Jesus commands the wind and sea to be still with the same divine authority this psalm ascribes to God.
options.note: Mark 4:39-41 records Jesus exercising exactly this authority, prompting the disciples' awe at who He must be.

options.text: It has no connection to any New Testament event.
options.note: The Gospel account of Jesus calming the storm directly echoes this psalm's themes.

options.text: It predicts a specific modern flood event.
options.note: The psalm's language is about God's timeless sovereignty over chaos, not a prediction of a specific modern event.

options.text: It anticipates God's ultimate authority over all creation.
options.note: This is true in a general sense, but the precise New Testament connection is the Gospel account of Jesus personally commanding the wind and sea to be still, Mark 4:39-41.

questions: This psalm declares that the LORD reigns now, not only someday. What circumstance in your life feels chaotic or out of control, and how does God's present reign speak into it?

The psalm pictures floodwaters roaring louder and louder, yet God remains greater still. What is 'roaring' the loudest in your life right now, and where are you tempted to believe it is louder than God?
Jesus exercised the very authority over the storm that this psalm ascribes to God alone. How does recognizing Jesus as this same reigning LORD change how you bring your fears to Him?
Verse 5 says God's testimonies, His decrees and promises, are fully confirmed. Which of God's promises do you most need to trust as firm and unshakeable this week?
The psalm ties God's holiness to His house 'for all the days to come.' How does the enduring holiness of God's presence shape the way you approach worship and daily life?

translationNotes.note: The LORD reigns translates a Hebrew verbal form emphasizing a settled, ongoing state, best understood as the LORD is reigning, a present and continuing reality.
The threefold repetition of the floods lifting up their voice mirrors, in Hebrew poetic style, the relentless and mounting sound of the rising waters.
Testimonies renders a term for God's solemn decrees or covenant stipulations, described here as being as firm and trustworthy as His eternal throne.
